item.title: Govt plans to upgrade Dhaka-Gazipur BRT corridor into six lanes
item.description:
The government has planned to convert the Dhaka-Gazipur Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) corridor into a six-lane conventional highway by removing BRT stations, lane dividers and associated infrastructure to ensure smoother and faster traffic movement.
Under the plan, three lanes will be allocated for general traffic in each direction. Two existing two-lane flyovers will also be upgraded to four lanes, an official familiar with the process said.
The issue was discussed at a cabinet meeting on October 18, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, according to a letter issued by the Road Transport and Highways Division on October 19.
The meeting decided to dissolve Dhaka Bus Rapid Transit PLC and transfer it under the Roads and Highways Department (RHD) for oversight.
The authorities concerned have been instructed to submit an initial progress report on implementing the decisions within 15 days, followed by updated reports by the third day of each month until implementation is complete, the letter said.
RHD Chief Engineer Md Moniruzzaman said the department had been informed of the government's decision and was taking the necessary steps.
He said an initial progress report would be submitted within 15 days, with further measures taken in line with government directives.
Approved in November 2012, the 20.5-kilometre BRT project was initially scheduled for completion by December 2016 at an estimated cost of Tk2,037.9 crore.
However, implementation delays and repeated revisions pushed the estimated cost to Tk4,268.32 crore, according to Moniruzzaman.
The project was financed by the Bangladesh government, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the French development agency Agence Française de Développement (AFD).
By December 2024, around 97% of the infrastructure work had been completed, while overall physical progress stood at 77.48%. The project tenure expired that month and was not extended.
Although the dedicated BRT lanes were subsequently opened to general traffic, the planned bus service could not be launched after two attempts to procure buses failed.
In July 2025, the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) rejected a proposal to increase the project cost to Tk6,598 crore and extend its tenure until December 2029. It also ordered an investigation into the project's design and feasibility study.
The government later considered four options for the corridor: completing the BRT project, introducing bus services under a route-franchising system, converting it into a toll-based expressway, or turning it into a conventional highway. It ultimately opted for the last option.
A review team from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) had recommended abandoning the planned BRT service, citing design flaws and limited capacity. The team suggested using the existing infrastructure for general traffic rather than making further investments.
In October 2025, the interim government also decided against launching BRT services on the route, citing the additional time and funding required.
The latest decision has, however, raised concerns among urban planners and civic organisations.
The Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP) described the move as a setback for sustainable and inclusive public transport and called for reconsideration.
The organisation said the decision was inconsistent with recommendations in the Gazipur Transport Master Plan and Dhaka's Revised Strategic Transport Plan (RSTP).
It warned that the move could prioritise private cars while failing to adequately address public transport needs in Gazipur and Uttara, whose residents have endured years of disruption due to construction work.
After years of delays and cost escalation, the corridor's conversion into a conventional highway will require careful planning to ease congestion, improve road safety and ensure that the existing infrastructure serves the wider public without undermining access to public transport.

item.title: Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for Ukraine war talks
item.description:
Russia’s Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff on ending the Ukraine war in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, with the American official saying he had brought “ideas” for a possible peace deal.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Norway, where he met Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky in talks Washington described as “positive.”
The meeting is taking place as the United States pushes an end to Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, with Russia pounding Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Donald Trump and Zelensky.
As Witkoff touched down in Putin’s home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump, and that it had freed a US citizen -- Stephen Hubbard -- held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a “mercenary” for Ukraine.
“We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure,” Witkoff -- Trump’s business partner and envoy -- told Putin in Saint Petersburg’s Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The longtime Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
“I’m hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what are those next steps,” he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his “attention” to the conflict and said the US leader had “insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict” in their last phone call.
Russia’s war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow’s strikes killed at least four people -- including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as “productive.”
“I think there’s some degree of momentum and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict,” he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday’s talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was “grateful” for a diesel deal -- met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe -- that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further “business and economic cooperation” with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
“We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over,” he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a “mercenary” fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a “humanitarian.”
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

item.title: BJKS: Road crashes claim over 125,000 lives from 2014 to June 2026
item.description:
At least 1,25,405 people were killed and 1,76,249 others injured in 72,736 road crashes across the country from 2014 to June 30, 2026, according to Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity (BJKS).
The organization disclosed the figures in a statement issued on Wednesday on the occasion of National Road Safety Day 2026, blaming mismanagement, irregularities and flawed policies in the road transport sector for the high toll.
It said the figures on crashes, casualties and their causes were compiled by monitoring media reports published between 2014 and June 30, 2026.
The BJKS also claimed that the actual number of casualties could be several times higher than the published figures.
It alleged that successive governments had focused on building and expanding roads since independence instead of developing an integrated transport system by increasing the use of waterways and railways.
As a result, dependence on roads has increased without a corresponding improvement in public transport or the development of an integrated transport network, the organization said.
BJKS Secretary General Mozammel Haque Chowdhury said the pressure of vehicles on roads has increased because of road-centric development that ignored strategic transport planning, and because of policies that shrank railways and waterways.
He also alleged that policy blunders, irregularities and corruption of the previous government contributed to the rise in road crashes.
The statement said chaos on roads is growing due to mismanagement in the transport sector, alleged extortion involving transport owners, workers and some police officials, the plying of unfit vehicles, unlicensed and unskilled drivers, flaws in road construction, and violations of traffic rules.
In its observations, the organization said the rapid increase in the number of motorcycles, battery-run rickshaws and CNG-run auto-rickshaws, and their unrestricted movement are one of the major causes of road crashes.
It also cited the absence of medians on roads, obstructed visibility at curves due to trees, structural defects in highways and vehicles, and disregard for traffic rules as contributing factors.
Driving on the wrong side, extortion on roads, carrying passengers in goods-laden vehicles, unskilled drivers, unfit vehicles and overloading of passengers also heightened the risk of accidents, BJKS said.
It further identified reckless speeding, dangerous overtaking, and driving for long hours without breaks or rest as significant causes of crashes.
To reduce road fatalities, the organisation recommended that the Ministry of Road Transport and Bridges and the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) be run under the supervision of local and foreign transport experts, instead of the bureaucratic system.
It also stressed building a modern, technology-based bus network across the country, in line with developed nations, and modernising road control systems through greater use of technology.
The recommendations call for issuing licences only after ensuring drivers' skills through modern, technology-based training.
The BJKS also suggested building footpaths and service lanes on important national highways, arranging safe road crossings for pedestrians, and installing necessary road signs and markings.
It emphasized ending extortion through structural reforms in the transport sector and fixing drivers' wages and working hours.
The organization also recommended ensuring quality road construction and repair, conducting regular road safety audits, and modernising the process of issuing vehicle fitness certificates.
It proposed withdrawing expired public transport vehicles from the roads, enhancing the institutional capacity of the BRTA, and establishing a traffic training academy for drivers.

item.title: Washington orders US embassy staff, families to leave Saudi Arabia
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-AIRPORT

Washington has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Wednesday, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

It came after a diplomatic source told AFP that “all American staff and their families have been ordered to depart from the US embassy” in the Gulf kingdom.

The source added that families of embassy staff had also been ordered to leave the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, all of which have been targeted by Iran during the Middle East war.

US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott subsequently confirmed the order in a post on X, but said it applied to “non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only”.

He linked the move to Houthi attacks on the country, including airports, saying “the safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority”.

Saudi Arabia has this month come under near-daily attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the kingdom’s deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.

On Wednesday, the Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured a further two.

“The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others,” the ministry said in a statement.

It did not say who launched the drone aimed at Shaybah oil field near the UAE border. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported intercepting six drones.

In June, a four-year-old truce in Yemen’s civil war collapsed, reviving the conflict that dates back to 2014. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the internationally recognised government since 2015.

Iran explosions

The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran and again in July before US President Donald Trump called off a new wave of strikes.

Late on Wednesday, Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a spell of relative calm.

“A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province,” the official IRNA news agency said.

It added that “local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions”.

The conflict began in late February, when the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, killing the country’s supreme leader, along with senior military commanders.

Iran has attempted to blockade the strategic waterway, demanding all ships seek its authorisation to cross. In peacetime, the Hormuz strait carried around a fifth of the world’s oil supplies.

In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships.

item.title: Pakistan-United States relations: Why Trump is sending “Thank You Pakistan” messages to Islamabad
item.description:
When the slogan “Thank You Pakistan” rang out in the Iranian parliament, most Pakistanis were delighted. But after trade with Iran was halted, Donald Trump began sending “Thank You Pakistan” messages to Islamabad. Public discontent in Pakistan is evident as these tactically worded expressions of gratitude have sparked fresh tensions with its neighbour. Hamid Mir has written about the matter.

In June 2025, "Thank You Pakistan" slogans rang out in the Iranian Parliament. The reason was obvious: Pakistan had not only condemned Israeli aggression against Iran but also supported it at every international forum. Pakistan again played a key role in brokering a ceasefire between Iran and the United States in April 2026, and once more several Iranian TV channels aired Persian songs saying "Thank You Pakistan." Iranians waved Pakistani flags at anti-US rallies in Tehran. The two countries opened several border crossings to promote trade, but this love affair came to an end on 17 October 2026.

The newspapers of October 18 carried the troubling report that Pakistan had temporarily closed its border crossings with Iran, including Gabd-Rimdan. Gabd lies in Pakistani Balochistan and Rimdan in Iranian Balochistan, and the crossing is just 87 kilometers from Gwadar Port. A few months ago, when tensions between Iran and the United States disrupted trade through the Strait of Hormuz, traffic at Gwadar suddenly increased.

As Gwadar grew in importance, trade between Pakistan and Iran also began through Gabd and Rimdan. Iranian companies and traders started ordering goods to Gwadar, and from there the cargo reached Iran in two hours. The crossing was also busier because it was safer than the Taftan-Zahedan border.

Now a spokesperson for the Balochistan government says the crossing was closed because of the poor law and order situation and smuggling. Iran's Foreign Ministry gave a cautious statement, saying the border has been closed temporarily for "technical reasons." Reports indicate that the situation is the same at Taftan-Zahedan, and thousands of containers are stuck at both crossings. Trade routes between Pakistan and India, and between Pakistan and Afghanistan, were already closed. With Iran's routes now shut as well, Gwadar Port will suffer the most. The closure may also raise liquefied gas prices in Pakistan, as more than 4,000 tonnes of LPG were entering the country daily through Gabd-Rimdan.

Gwadar is only 400 kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world''s oil trade passes. Tensions over Hormuz temporarily increased Gwadar''s importance, but sadly the Pakistani government seems to be struggling to sustain it. The port is needed not only by Iran but also by many countries of South Asia, Central Asia, and West Asia. In 2019, Saudi Arabia's Aramco expressed interest in building a ten-billion-dollar oil refinery here. The Saudi company wanted China to join the project as a partner, but the talks did not progress. The Chinese have been under attack in Balochistan since 2013, and Pakistan accuses India and Afghanistan of cross-border terrorism there. Pakistan shares more than 2600 kilometers border with Afghanistan and 900 kilometers border with Iran.

The Saudis wanted Chinese partnership in Gwadar to address security concerns, but China declined for several reasons, not least that it never wanted to offend Iran. Since the Iran-America war the refinery project has been stalled, and after the recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia its prospects have diminished further. Gwadar is only 87 kilometers from Iran, and Pakistan is part of a joint defense alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. Iranian-backed Houthis have targeted Aramco in Saudi Arabia many times. They could do the same in Pakistan.

Ever since work began on Gwadar Port under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), terrorism in Balochistan has increased. Not just one enemy country is behind it; some friendly Gulf countries also have a hand, as they fear Gwadar's development will affect their own ports. To put an end to these conspiracies, Pakistan some time ago offered the United States the chance to develop Pasni Port, only one hundred kilometers from Gwadar. But US authorities seem more interested in the mineral wealth of Balochistan than in developing Pasni. The Makran coast has not only Gwadar and Pasni but also the ports of Jiwani, Ormara, and Sonmiani. Balochistan has both coastline and resources, yet because of bad governance and terrorism, no improvement in its situation is visible.

I still remember that when Dr. Shireen Mazari was head of the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad, President General Pervez Musharraf told us there that he was handing over the blue waters of Gwadar to China, and that it would now be for China and India to deal with each other. Former Foreign Minister Agha Shahi was not at all pleased to hear this. Puffing vigorously on his pipe, he told me that China was certainly our friend, but if Gwadar Port were handed over without an effective strategy, Balochistan would become a center of international conspiracies.

One great tragedy of Pakistan is that our rulers have no knowledge of the history of its provinces and important regions. History is deeply connected with geography, and if lessons are not learned from history, geography changes. Our rulers must read the history of Gwadar and the Makran coast. Sahil-e-Makran, by Professor Dr. Hameed Baloch of Lasbela University, Uthal, Balochistan, should be read by every policymaker and every student of history in Pakistan. This two-volume work is a treasure not only of knowledge but also of historical documents, which show that British forces used small airfields along the Makran coast to attack Japanese forces.

Many years ago, when I first went to Gwadar, the elders showed me their old passports issued by the Sultanate of Oman. Gwadar remained part of Oman until 1958, when, on 6 September, a weak political government under Malik Feroz Khan Noon paid three million British pounds to bring it into Pakistan. The Khan of Kalat, Nasir Khan I, had given Gwadar in 1783 to a rebel prince of Muscat, and later tried to take it back without success. The Omani government earned considerable profit from the taxes levied at Gwadar Port. The Khan of Kalat then reduced taxes at the ports of Pasni and Jiwani, which diminished Gwadar's importance, after which the British government began to consider handing Gwadar over to Kalat. Some British oil companies, unhappy with the rulers of Oman, also played an important role in this.

Dr. Hameed Baloch also writes that, after the creation of Pakistan, All India Radio one day broadcast a false report that the Khan of Kalat had decided to merge his state with India. The Khan, Ahmad Yar Khan, immediately sent a telegram to Viceroy Lord Mountbatten asking that the report be denied. Reacting to this false news, he decided to accede to Pakistan in March 1948, and with the accession of Kalat, Pasni and Jiwani also came under Pakistan's control. In 1954, the US Geological Survey declared Gwadar a great port of the future.

The Omani government wanted to hand Gwadar over to India, but India was then more interested in Goa. India took Goa by military action, while Pakistan acquired Gwadar from Oman through negotiation. The political government that brought Gwadar into Pakistan was removed within weeks, when General Ayub Khan imposed martial law in October 1958. Gwadar was incorporated into Pakistan, but the fortunes of Gwadar and Balochistan have not changed to this day. A few days ago the establishment imposed Governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to fight terrorism, yet the situation in Balochistan is worse than in KP.

The sudden decision to close the Gabd-Rimdan crossing has caused turmoil and uproar not only in Gwadar but all over Balochistan. The cries of Baloch businessmen have reached me through officials of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, but perhaps they have not reached the rulers in Islamabad. There is an impression that Pakistan closed its trade routes with Iran under American pressure. This closure may help the US, but it is definitely hurting Pakistan.

Remember: until there is stability on the Makran coast, Balochistan will not be stable, and if Balochistan is not stable, Pakistan cannot move forward. Pakistan should not act like a proxy of the US, nor become a source of pleasure for Israel. Tension between Pakistan and Iran will please Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu. When "Thank You Pakistan" slogans were raised in the Iranian Parliament, the majority of Pakistanis were very happy.

After the closure of trade with Iran, Donald Trump is sending "Thank You Pakistan" messages to Islamabad. We cannot hear this mischievous thank-you, but we can see the unhappiness in Pakistan over a new tension with another neighbor. Pakistanis were happy to mediate between Iran and US but they will not accept collaboration with US against Iran. I hope that recent visit of Pakistani head of the Armed Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir to Iran will remove misunderstandings between the countries and Pakistan will restrict only to a mediator.

*Hamid Mir is a Pakistani journalist.

item.description:
“Resource curse” refers to an economic and political situation in which a country, despite possessing abundant natural resources (such as oil, gas, gold, or diamonds), fails to achieve the desired level of economic development. Instead, it suffers from economic stagnation, instability, and corruption. This phenomenon is often referred to as the “paradox of plenty.” Is Bangladesh experiencing such a paradox in relation to Chittagong Port?

The fact that there are arguments in favour of appointing a foreign operator does not place the decision to entrust a particular company with long-term operations under specific terms beyond scrutiny

A port’s depth is measured by its navigability, but the depth of a state is reflected in the transparency of its decision-making. The question of handing over the operation of Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) to a foreign company for 15 years is therefore not merely a matter of efficiency, investment, or profit. It is also a question of the public’s rights over state assets and of democratic accountability in decisions concerning those assets.

Recently, an agreement was signed with DP World, a company from the United Arab Emirates, concerning the operation of the New Mooring Container Terminal. But why was such a major national economic decision not discussed in parliament? Why was there no perceived need for meaningful parliamentary debate on the terms of the agreement, the financial gains and losses for the state, the future of the hundreds of port workers, and questions of national security?

These questions do not arise from opposition to foreign investment; rather, they stem from a demand for democratic accountability in decisions as important as investment. An agreement may be legally valid, but that does not mean every decision it entails automatically passes the test of serving the public interest. Particularly when a decision will have implications extending beyond the tenure of the current government and spanning the next 15 years, parliamentary discussion is not a mere formality, it is part of the state’s responsibility.

Modernising the port, but on what terms?

Improving the efficiency of Chittagong Port is essential. Vessel waiting times, delays in container handling, lengthy customs procedures, and limitations in road and rail connectivity increase the cost of imports and exports. The technology, experience, and professional management of an international operator could help address some of these problems.

There is no reason to automatically conclude that a foreign company is necessarily acting against the national interest. However, the fact that there are arguments in favour of appointing a foreign operator does not place the decision to entrust a particular company with long-term operations under specific terms beyond scrutiny. On the contrary, the greater the need for investment, the greater the importance of contractual transparency and competition.

According to information published in the media, DP World is expected to invest $150 million in operating and modernizing the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT). Of this amount, $50 million is to be paid to the port authority as a one-time payment. The contract term is 15 years. Under the revenue-sharing arrangement, the port authority is reportedly expected to receive between 40 and 67 per cent of the revenue per container. In addition, reports indicate that the authority will receive a fixed annual fee.

Foreign operator at Chittagong Port: What's in the agreement, what are the pros and cons?

These figures are important, but they are not sufficient to assess the entire agreement. Alongside the investment amount, it is necessary to know the terminal’s current revenue and expenditure, how net income will be calculated under the new arrangement, who will bear the operating costs, who will have the authority to revise tariffs, and in what condition the assets and technology will be returned to the state when the contract expires.

The most important question is that the NCT is an already operational terminal in which the government has made substantial investments. According to published information, the total investment in the terminal, including construction and equipment installation, amounts to Tk 27.12 billion. In the last fiscal year, it handled 1.385 million containers. So, how was the financial value of this existing capacity assessed? Was the alternative of continuing operations under domestic management examined with equal seriousness? The state cannot simply look at the potential revenue under the proposed arrangement; it must also calculate how much revenue could have been generated under alternative arrangements.

Parliamentary discussion is essential

This is where the issue moves beyond the confines of a commercial agreement and becomes a question of democratic governance. Parliament is the principal institution responsible for overseeing the state budget, expenditure, policies, and the accountability of the executive branch. It would not be appropriate to insist, without a legal basis, that every commercial agreement must receive parliamentary approval. But whether Parliament should discuss the long-term operation of a strategic asset such as the country’s largest container terminal is an entirely different question. From the standpoint of democratic accountability, the answer is clearly "yes".

It is worth noting that Article 145A of the Constitution of Bangladesh provides for treaties concluded with foreign states to be laid before Parliament. In this context, it is important to recognise that the political and democratic necessity of parliamentary discussion is not the same as a legal obligation to hold such a discussion. Given the port’s strategic importance, the case for parliamentary accountability is compelling; however, that importance does not automatically create a constitutional obligation.

Nevertheless, parliamentary discussion would have required the government to answer several fundamental questions. Why was an agreement with a specific company chosen instead of an open, competitive tendering process for this terminal? Why were proposals from domestic companies not considered? Were alternative proposals comparatively assessed in terms of investment, revenue, technology, workers’ rights, and security? Which clauses of the agreement cannot be disclosed, and why? These questions are not intended to oppose the government; they are necessary to scrutinize its decisions in light of the public interest.

When decisions are made about nationally important assets, the parliament must not be treated merely as a “platform” for presenting information. Parliamentary debate provides an opportunity to scrutinise the executive branch’s decisions, enables opposition parties to present alternative arguments, and helps the public understand the reasoning for and against a decision.

Even if it is not possible to disclose every commercial clause of an agreement, Parliament could at least have discussed its basic financial structure, the state’s liabilities, the risks involved, the extent of control, and the long-term implications. Commercial confidentiality may be necessary for strategic reasons, but confidentiality must not become a means of evading accountability.

In this context, the “public trust doctrine”, which concerns the state’s fiduciary responsibility for public resources, is a relevant concept. The central principle of this doctrine is that, when managing resources that affect the public interest, the state cannot simply exercise its discretion as an owner; it must also act as a responsible trustee charged with protecting the public interest. In the case of strategic infrastructure such as Chittagong Port, this concept reminds us that even if operational responsibility is transferred to a private company, the state cannot shirk its duty to safeguard the public interest.

Is a foreign operator the only way to efficiency?

The involvement of foreign companies in port operations is an internationally recognised arrangement. World Bank publications on port reform, along with international experience in port management, demonstrate that terminals can be operated by private companies while ownership remains with the government. Under such arrangements, efficiency and productivity have increased at many ports around the world.

However, the model of port management and the method of selecting an operator are two different matters. Under the “landlord model,” the public authority retains ownership of the land and basic infrastructure, while a private company undertakes investment and operations under a contract. This model can also be implemented through an open, competitive tendering process. Therefore, appointing a foreign operator should not automatically be equated with greater efficiency.

The challenges facing Chittagong Port are not confined to the terminals themselves. Waiting times for ships to berth, river navigability, customs clearance, delays in cargo handling, and inadequate road and rail connectivity all affect overall efficiency. An operator may be able to increase the speed of container handling within a terminal, but it cannot resolve administrative complications in customs or traffic congestion outside the port.

Therefore, alongside entrusting operations to a foreign company, the government must digitise customs procedures, increase container transportation by rail and waterways, modernize the port’s information systems, and strengthen the capacity of state regulatory institutions. If the state’s own capacity remains weak while dependence on a foreign company’s expertise increases, enforcing the state’s contractual rights may eventually become difficult, even when those rights are formally stipulated in the agreement.

Lessons from Doraleh Port

The dispute between DP World and the government of Djibouti over the Doraleh Container Terminal is an important international example. Following a dispute over a long-term concession agreement, the Djiboutian government terminated the contract in 2018 and took control of the terminal. The dispute subsequently escalated to international arbitration and courts. Questions concerning breaches of contract, the recognition of arbitral decisions, and remedies arose at various stages of the legal proceedings.

There is no need to label DP World a good or bad company on the basis of this experience. Rather, the lesson is that port operation agreements can sometimes become sources of long-term financial liabilities for states and give rise to complex international legal disputes.

One point must be kept in mind: governments change and policy priorities shift, but the obligations arising from contracts entered into by the state do not disappear easily.
It is therefore essential to understand the provisions of the NCT agreement concerning dispute resolution, the seat of arbitration, applicable law, conditions for contract termination, compensation, state intervention on national security grounds, and the restoration of operational control to the state in emergencies. It is not enough for the state’s rights to be written into the contract; the state must also possess the legal and administrative capacity to enforce them effectively.

Workers’ rights and public interest

The concerns raised by workers’ organisations regarding the NCT cannot be ignored. The government has stated that existing officers and employees are not at risk of losing their jobs and that modernisation could create additional employment opportunities. How far these assurances will hold up in practice will depend on the terms of the agreement and how it is implemented. Workers’ job security, training, working conditions, and opportunities to adapt to technological changes must be ensured.

At the same time, the concerns of businesses must also be taken seriously. If tariffs rise as the operator improves efficiency, the cost of imports and exports could increase. Ultimately, consumers and producers will bear the burden of those additional costs.

Therefore, efficiency cannot be assessed solely by counting how many containers are handled per hour. It is also necessary to examine how much service quality improves, whether ship waiting times decrease, whether business costs fall, whether workers’ rights remain protected, and how much the state’s net revenue increases.

Transparency and accountability are essential

Once the agreement has been concluded, the government’s greatest responsibility is to ensure public trust. Information that cannot be disclosed for reasons of national security or commercial confidentiality may reasonably be withheld. However, the key terms concerning investment, revenue sharing, tariff-setting, performance targets, workers’ rights, contract termination, and compensation should not be concealed from the public.

The government should present the main provisions of the agreement to parliament and arrange for the relevant parliamentary committee to review its financial, legal, security-related, and labour-related aspects. The agreement’s financial benefits and risks should be assessed through an independent audit. The results of periodic evaluations of the operator’s performance should also be made public.

There can be no disagreement over the need to modernise Chittagong Port; foreign investment may also be necessary. But accountability must not be weakened in the name of modernisation, nor should the state’s own capacity be allowed to erode in exchange for promises of greater efficiency.

The failure to discuss the long-term agreement concerning the country’s most important port in Parliament is therefore not merely a procedural shortcoming; it raises fundamental questions about how the state makes decisions. If development is intended to serve the public interest, what is the difficulty in presenting the rationale for that development to the people’s elected representatives?

Responsibility for port operations can be transferred through a contract. But responsibility for decisions concerning the country’s economic future cannot be handed over to an operator. That responsibility rests with the government, Parliament, and ultimately, the state itself.

The debate over Chittagong Port, therefore, is not about foreign versus domestic companies. The real question is how transparent and accountable the state is in its pursuit of efficiency, and how capable it is of protecting its own interests. A port may be leased to a foreign company, but the state’s responsibilities, the people’s rights, and the national interest cannot be leased out.

item.title: Bangladesh’s roads: 66 lives lost, 104 people permanently disabled on average every day
item.description:
Zahidul Alam, from Boalkhali in Chattogram, was working in Oman. He returned to Bangladesh on leave in August 2024. On 4 September, a motorcycle accident left his arms and legs fractured. His jaw was damaged, three teeth were broken, and he sustained a serious head injury.

He received prolonged treatment at Chattogram Medical College Hospital and later at Evercare Hospital Chattogram. Although his life was saved, he could not escape permanent disability.

Zahidul, 28, is now receiving treatment in Bengaluru, India. Speaking to Prothom Alo by phone from Bengaluru last Tuesday, he said he had exhausted all his savings.

He has already spent Tk 6.5 million on treatment and had to borrow money to cover the costs. He has not been able to return abroad and fears he never will. He said he had undergone eight operations on his leg, which had developed gangrene several times.

Like Zahidul, many people injured in road accidents are forced to endure lives of hardship. A large proportion of the injured are young people and working-age adults. The consequences also affect their families.

Another road accident victim is Md Sajib, from Rupganj in Narayanganj. He was involved in a motorcycle accident on the Dhaka–Mawa Expressway in 2021. His left leg was broken, and he sustained injuries to various parts of his body.

He received treatment at Dhaka’s National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopaedic Rehabilitation (NITOR), commonly known as the Pangu Hospital, for about 33 days and underwent surgery. He still cannot walk normally.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on Tuesday, Sajib said he had worked at a factory before the accident. He was unable to work for nearly three years afterwards. He now runs a tea stall and struggles to make ends meet.

A survey conducted in 2023–24 by the Centre for Injury Prevention and Research, Bangladesh (CIPRB), under the Directorate General of Health Services’ Non-Communicable Disease Control programme, found that more than three million people are injured in road accidents each year.

Of them, around 38,000 suffer permanent disabilities. That amounts to an average of 104 people becoming permanently disabled every day. Road accidents also claim an average of 66 lives daily.

According to the National Health and Injury Survey, around 16.574 million people in Bangladesh suffer non-fatal injuries from various causes every year. Of these, 3,031,028 are injured in road accidents.

Data collection for the survey, titled National Health and Injury Survey, began in May 2023 and continued until mid-February 2024. A summary report was published in February 2024. The survey covered all 64 districts and analysed information from 442,998 people.

The survey found that road accidents are the leading cause of injury-related deaths in Bangladesh. Among causes of non-fatal injuries, road accidents rank third.

Against this backdrop, National Road Safety Day is being observed in Bangladesh today, 22 October. This year’s theme is “Safe Roads, a Prosperous Country: Bangladesh First”. The main event will not take place today, however; official observances have been rescheduled for 28 October because of the Durga Puja holiday.

Over 3 million people injured on roads every year

According to the National Health and Injury Survey, around 16.574 million people in Bangladesh suffer non-fatal injuries from various causes every year. Of these, 3,031,028 are injured in road accidents.

In other words, road accidents account for about 18.3 per cent of all non-fatal injuries. Every year, approximately 1,835 people per 100,000 population are injured in road accidents.

The survey estimates that around 24,233 people die in road accidents in Bangladesh each year, an average of 66 a day. The annual road accident death rate is 14.67 per 100,000 people. Men account for 84.6 per cent of those killed, while women make up 15.4 per cent.

The survey also highlights the long-term consequences of injuries that leave people permanently disabled. Permanent disability is one of the most serious outcomes of road accidents. According to the findings, around 138,689 people in Bangladesh become permanently disabled each year as a result of different types of injuries.

Of these, 38,028 people suffer permanent disabilities every year because of road accidents—an average of 104 a day. Road accidents account for about 27.4 per cent of all permanent disabilities caused by injuries in the country. For the purposes of the survey, permanent disability included lasting impairment of vision, hearing, hand function, mobility or mental functioning.

In 2021, a head-on collision between a bus and a microbus in Rajshahi caused the microbus to catch fire, killing 17 people. All the passengers in the microbus belonged to the same family. Pavel Mia was the only survivor, losing his parents and other relatives. He was 17 at the time and had just enrolled at Rangpur Police Lines School and College.

Many are from low-income households and are the main earners in their families. When they become disabled, they can face severe hardship, placing additional pressure on their families and the state.

Pavel spent three months in intensive care after the accident. He permanently lost two teeth and the thumb of his right hand. His speech remains slurred, and he could not continue his education. Speaking to Prothom Alo, Pavel said he was unable to work and that a government job would help him support himself.

Nearly 85pc of road accident victims killed are men

The survey estimates that around 24,233 people die in road accidents in Bangladesh each year, an average of 66 a day. The annual road accident death rate is 14.67 per 100,000 people. Men account for 84.6 per cent of those killed, while women make up 15.4 per cent.

The survey found that the road accident death rate is higher in urban areas than in rural areas. In cities, the rate is 16.56 deaths per 100,000 people, compared with 13.81 in rural areas.

Salim Mahmud Chowdhury, deputy executive director of CIPRB, told Prothom Alo that most people killed, seriously injured or permanently disabled in road accidents are young. Many are from low-income households and are the main earners in their families.

When they become disabled, they can face severe hardship, placing additional pressure on their families and the state, he added.

Salim Mahmud Chowdhury called for greater emphasis on legislation, enforcement and public awareness to reduce accidents.

Why are there so many accidents?

Various studies and government reports have identified several causes of road accidents, including reckless and excessive speeding, inattention, dangerous overtaking, traffic law violations, drivers’ lack of skills, physical or mental illness, fatigue, driving while drowsy and using mobile phones while driving.

Other risk factors include defective and unfit vehicles, faulty brakes, overloading of passengers and goods, uncontrolled movement of slow-moving vehicles on highways, risky motorcycle use and careless pedestrian behaviour.

Samsul Hoque, Professor in the Department of Civil Engineering at BUETReducing road accidents required tackling the problems at their roots. Vehicle fitness certification and route permits, as well as the process of issuing drivers’ licences, must be made effective, and monitoring must be strengthened at the field level. Plans should be developed by analysing data and evidence.

Poor road design, dangerous bends, inadequate street lighting, insufficient signs and signals, a lack of safety measures, the absence of road dividers and safe crossing facilities, and inadequate roadside protection also contribute to deaths and serious injuries.

The failure to use helmets, seat belts and child safety equipment, insufficient rest and excessive working hours for drivers, weak traffic management, lax law enforcement, inadequate oversight and institutional capacity at the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA), and delays in receiving prompt, quality medical care after an accident further increase the risk of death.

Experts, however, say Bangladesh lacks the specific plan needed to reduce road accidents. The National Road Safety Council is the country’s highest-level forum for preventing road accidents. What is the government doing?

The United Nations has declared 2021–2030 the Decade of Action for Road Safety. Its main goal is to reduce road deaths and injuries worldwide by 50 per cent by 2030. The UN General Assembly adopted the initiative in 2020. A global plan developed under the coordination of the World Health Organization emphasises safer road infrastructure, vehicle safety, speed management, law enforcement and prompt medical care after accidents.

A high-level meeting on road safety was held at UN headquarters in New York on 20 and 21 July. Bangladesh was represented by Road Transport and Bridges Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam.

At the meeting, Shaikh Rabiul Alam outlined Bangladesh’s commitment to improving road safety. He referred to initiatives involving artificial intelligence-based speed control, rapid emergency medical care after accidents and improved pedestrian safety. He also pledged to enact an integrated road safety law by 2027.

Speaking to Prothom Alo yesterday, the minister said the government had adopted a firm position against allowing unroadworthy vehicles on the roads and was working to control vehicle speeds. He expressed hope that road accidents and fatalities could be halved by 2030.

Road Transport and Bridges Minister Shaikh Rabiul AlamThe government had adopted a firm position against allowing unroadworthy vehicles on the roads and was working to control vehicle speeds. Road accidents and fatalities could be halved by 2030.

He further said the laws and regulations needed to make roads safer would be introduced by 2027.

The transport sector had been disorderly for a long time, he added, and bringing it under control overnight would be difficult. Some time would be needed.

He also expected the situation to improve considerably once a World Bank-funded project was implemented.

Experts, however, say Bangladesh lacks the specific plan needed to reduce road accidents. The National Road Safety Council is the country’s highest-level forum for preventing road accidents. It met only once during the interim government’s nearly 18-month tenure, and no meeting has yet been held under the current government, despite the requirement for the council to meet every six months.

The BRTA and the Roads and Highways Department (RHD) have road safety divisions or units tasked with addressing road accidents. Their activities, however, remain largely limited to distributing leaflets and organising events on designated days.

The RHD is implementing a World Bank-funded road safety project. Its main objectives are to reduce road deaths and serious injuries and strengthen the capacity of government agencies responsible for road safety management.

The project was approved at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) on 18 April 2023. It has a total budget of Tk 49.88 billion and is scheduled to run until June 2028.

Samsul Hoque, a professor in the Department of Civil Engineering at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) and a transport specialist, told Prothom Alo that the government had yet to adopt a concrete plan to halve road accidents and fatalities.

“Promises alone will not work. No matter how much is said, nothing will change without an innovative, scientific and sustainable plan,” he said.

Samsul Hoque said reducing road accidents required tackling the problems at their roots. Vehicle fitness certification and route permits, as well as the process of issuing drivers’ licences, must be made effective, and monitoring must be strengthened at the field level.

Plans should be developed by analysing data and evidence, he added.

item.title: LNG terminal in the Sundarbans could increase environmental risks
item.description:
The Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, is facing multiple challenges due to climate change, industries centred around Mongla and pollution from the Rampal power plant, among other factors. Amid this situation, Akram Point, an ecologically important area inside the Sundarbans, and Nolian village adjacent to the forest are being considered as potential sites for an LNG (liquefied natural gas) terminal to address the country's energy crisis.

Akram Point is the confluence of the Shibsa and Pashur rivers inside the Sundarbans. Within two kilometres of this point, the Sundarbans South Wildlife Sanctuary lies on one side and the Sundarbans East Wildlife Sanctuary on the other. Both sanctuaries are part of the World Heritage Site declared by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).

Another wildlife sanctuary is located within two kilometres of Nolian village, opposite the village along the Shibsa River. Although Nolian is not part of the Sundarbans, it falls within the Ecologically Critical Area (ECA), which covers a 10-kilometre zone surrounding the forest.

On 13 August, Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud announced at an event that three floating LNG terminals would be built at Hiron Point in Khulna, Mongla and Payra.

Later, on 19 October, Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said at an event organised by the Foreign Investors' Chamber of Commerce and Industry at a hotel in the capital that an LNG terminal would be built at a location near Khulna with a draft of 20 metres.

Akram Point is the confluence of the Shibsa and Pashur rivers inside the Sundarbans. Within two kilometres of this point, the Sundarbans South Wildlife Sanctuary lies on one side and the Sundarbans East Wildlife Sanctuary on the other.

A forest expert, on condition of anonymity, told Prothom Alo that it remains to be seen which method the Energy Ministry would use to lay the pipeline.

According to him, the conventional open-cut method would not be feasible. The underground breathing roots of trees would be damaged, causing many trees to die.

Pointing out that an alternative would be to lay the pipeline beneath the roots, but that would be extremely expensive, he said, "The government may not opt for that method in an effort to reduce costs."

Aninda Islam Amit, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, told Prothom Alo that the south-western region of the country had long been deprived of development. Industrialisation was essential to improving the lives of people in the region.

He further said the prime minister is visiting Khulna to assess plans for modernising Mongla Port, establishing the economic zone proposed by the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority (BEZA), and developing tourism in the Sundarbans. By seeing the area first-hand, she would be able to understand how these issues were interconnected.

The state minister added that feasibility studies and environmental assessments would be conducted before any such initiatives were pursued. Only if the findings proved favourable would there be scope for further discussions on these proposals, he said.

Minister and adviser visit Akram Point

The government's Finance and Planning Adviser, ministers and the chairman of the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority (BEZA) have visited Akram Point several times to assess the feasibility of constructing a terminal there. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is also scheduled to visit the Sundarbans today, Thursday. State Minister Aninda Islam had also mentioned the initiative to establish a new LNG terminal in a Facebook post on 14 August.

Aninda Islam Amit, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral ResourcesThe south-western region of the country had long been deprived of development. Industrialisation was essential to improving the lives of people in the region.

Two days later, on 16 August, a high-level government delegation comprising Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir; Energy Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud; Shipping, Road Transport, Bridges and Railways Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam; and BEZA Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, among others, visited Akram Point in the Bay of Bengal, the Shibsa River, the Sundarbans and Mongla Port. The chairman of the Mongla Port Authority was also part of the delegation.

After the visit, Shaikh Rabiul Alam said at a reception organised by the Mongla municipal BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) at the Mongla Port bus stand that afternoon that a floating LNG station would be established at Akram Point of Mongla Port. A 23-kilometre pipeline would be laid to bring gas to Mongla, which would then be used to generate electricity.

Asked for his opinion, M Firoz Ahmed, former professor of the Department of Civil Engineering at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) and vice-president of Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon (BAPA), told Prothom Alo, "Whenever something is built inside a forest, there will inevitably be an impact, no matter how much anyone claims otherwise. Since the Sundarbans is our World Heritage Site, the government should reconsider this decision."

Firoz Ahmed further said that since gas is a flammable substance, the possibility of accidents cannot be ruled out. If an accident occurs, the Sundarbans will be affected.

During the process of converting LNG into gas, large quantities of cold or hot water would have to be discharged into the river. This would change the river water temperature and disrupt the process of photosynthesis. Fish eggs and fry could consequently be destroyed.

Recalling that there were several incidents of oil spills from ships in the past, he said a terminal would increase ship movements, which could also lead to oil leaks and spills. The more ships move through the area, the greater the pollution will be.

Forest department objects

The Department of Forest, under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, is the legal authority responsible for the conservation and maintenance of the Sundarbans. Although senior government officials have visited the proposed site for the terminal, the forest department has not been informed either formally or informally.

Asked about the matter, Chief Conservator of Forests Md Amir Hossain Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that the ministry had not informed the department about the proposed terminal. He declined to make any further comment.

Meanwhile, after learning about the proposed terminal through various sources, the office of the Conservator of Forests in Khulna recently sent a letter to the Forest Department expressing concern.

The letter said reports from various sources indicated that an LNG terminal would be established at Akram Point within the Sundarbans World Heritage Site. LNG would be supplied to the terminal through pipelines from the deep sea.

Akram Point and the surrounding forest areas are natural habitats where tigers and other wildlife roam freely. Construction activities for the terminal, artificial lighting and industrial operations would disrupt the natural breeding and movement of tigers, spotted deer and wild boars.

Akram Point is located close to the South Wildlife Sanctuary. As wildlife sanctuary areas lie on both sides of Akram Point, establishing a terminal there would have severe and long-term impacts on the vegetation, wildlife and overall ecosystem of this unique mangrove forest.

Further concerns raised in the letter

The letter noted that the movement of huge LNG carriers and ships would generate intense noise and vibration. As a result, the endangered Irrawaddy and Ganges river dolphins could lose their habitats. These aquatic animals could also be killed by collisions with the propellers of ships and tankers.

During the process of converting LNG into gas, large quantities of cold or hot water would have to be discharged into the river. This would change the river water temperature and disrupt the process of photosynthesis. Fish eggs and fry could consequently be destroyed.

Akram Point and the surrounding forest areas are natural habitats where tigers and other wildlife roam freely. Construction activities for the terminal, artificial lighting and industrial operations would disrupt the natural breeding and movement of tigers, spotted deer and wild boars.

M Firoz Ahmed, Former professor, Department of Civil Engineering, BUET and VP of BAPAWhenever something is built inside a forest, there will inevitably be an impact, no matter how much anyone claims otherwise. Since the Sundarbans is our World Heritage Site, the government should reconsider this decision.

The mudflats of the mangrove forest are habitats for numerous migratory birds and amphibians. Construction of the terminal would destroy these mudflats and, consequently, their habitats.

One of the major concerns raised in the letter relates to sundari and other mangrove tree species in the Sundarbans. If a terminal is established at Akram Point or Nolian, regular dredging would be required to facilitate ship movements. This would cause heavy metals deposited on riverbeds by industries to mix with river water. The breathing roots of mangrove trees would also become buried under sediment.

As a result, sundari, gewa and goran trees would die because they could no longer breathe. In addition, burnt oil and chemical waste discharged from ships could reach the forest floor and permanently disrupt the natural process of seedling regeneration.

UNESCO's latest meeting

UNESCO has been monitoring the condition of the Sundarbans since 2014. The latest meeting of the World Heritage Committee to review the overall condition of World Heritage Sites was held on 21 July in Busan, South Korea. Several decisions concerning the Sundarbans were taken during the 10-day meeting.

The World Heritage Centre provides technical assistance to the World Heritage Committee in assessing the overall condition of World Heritage Sites. In its report, the centre sought updated information from the Bangladesh delegation on the implementation of recommendations made by a joint UNESCO and International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) mission in 2019.

Following the joint mission's recommendations, Bangladesh prepared a Strategic Environmental Assessment report for the southwestern region, including the Sundarbans. However, the World Heritage Centre criticised Bangladesh for not conducting detailed research on the Sundarbans as part of that assessment, despite its recommendation to do so.

According to the draft report of the World Heritage Centre, the centre urged Bangladesh to implement a Strategic Environmental Management Plan to address the direct and indirect threats identified for the Sundarbans over the next 20 years. It also emphasised the need for further research and data collection to assess the impacts on the Sundarbans in accordance with the management plan.

The World Heritage Centre also said that any decision to establish large industries around the Sundarbans should follow the guidelines of the World Heritage Convention to protect the forest's Outstanding Universal Value.

Bangladesh was asked to submit a report on the conservation status of the Sundarbans by 1 December 2027.

However, Azerbaijan proposed amendments to these recommendations at the World Heritage Committee meeting. In line with that proposal, the deadline for submitting the report on the Sundarbans was extended from December 2027 to February 2029.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Humaiun Kobir, met Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov in Baku on 16 October. During the meeting, Azerbaijan expressed interest in investing in Bangladesh’s energy sector.

Rampal, UNESCO’s opposition and risks the Sundarbans facing

Environmental and forestry experts say the decision to install an LNG terminal could prompt UNESCO to remove the Sundarbans from the World Heritage List.

According to them, pollution from industries centred around Mongla and the Rampal power plant has already affected the Sundarbans’ wildlife and ecosystem in various ways. They believe that such energy infrastructure would expose the mangrove forest to even greater risks.

During the ousted Awami League government’s tenure, UNESCO strongly opposed the construction of a coal-fired power plant in Rampal, Bagerhat. At one point, it considered placing the Sundarbans on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

At the 38th session of the World Heritage Committee, held in Doha in 2014, UNESCO expressed concern over the Rampal power plant and the industrial development planned in the surrounding area.

The committee’s decision stated that it was unclear whether the potential indirect impacts of the power plant on the Sundarbans had been adequately assessed. The meeting in Doha also raised concerns about the development of other industries and infrastructure in the vicinity.

From 22 to 28 March 2016, a joint monitoring mission from the UNESCO World Heritage Centre and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) visited the Sundarbans. In an assessment published on 18 October that year, the Rampal power plant was identified as a serious threat to the Sundarbans, and the mission recommended cancelling the project and relocating it elsewhere.

At the time, UNESCO’s assessment found that the environmental impact assessment conducted by the then government had failed to adequately consider the risks the power plant would pose to the Sundarbans.

Although the government then decided to provide UNESCO with all the information and data relating to the power plant, it remained adamant that the facility would not be relocated.

Subsequently, at a UNESCO meeting in 2018, the government was warned against approving industrial projects before conducting a strategic environmental assessment of the Sundarbans.

item.title: Bangladesh improves in rule of law index but trails several African nations
item.description:
Bangladesh has made a slight improvement in its overall rule of law score but continues to rank below several African countries, including Kenya, Zimbabwe and Nigeria, according to the Rule of Law Index 2026 released on Wednesday.
Bangladesh ranked 123rd among 143 countries and jurisdictions in the World Justice Project (WJP) index, behind Zimbabwe (122nd), Nigeria (120th), Sierra Leone (110th), Liberia (103rd), Kenya (100th) and Ghana (62nd).
Its score increased by 0.6% to 0.393 out of 1, up from 0.391 in 2025, making Bangladesh the world's 15th-biggest improver and South Asia's top gainer. Its ranking improved by two places from 125th, although its score remained below the global average of 0.55.
The index assesses countries across eight factors: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice.
Bangladesh improved in only three factors — constraints on government powers, absence of corruption and regulatory enforcement — while its performance declined in the other five.
Fundamental rights remained the country's weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 133rd and scoring 0.30, placing it among the 11 lowest-ranked countries.
The indicator assesses the protection of fundamental human rights under international law. Civil justice was the second-weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 132nd and scoring 0.36. The indicator measures access to and the effectiveness of the civil justice system in resolving grievances.
Bangladesh ranked 124th in regulatory enforcement, with a score of 0.40, and 117th in criminal justice, scoring 0.32. In the absence of corruption category, which measures bribery, improper influence and the misappropriation of public resources, it ranked 113th with a score of 0.35.
The country ranked 111th in constraints on government powers, which measures accountability under the law, with a score of 0.38.
Open government was Bangladesh's highest-ranked factor at 106th, with a score of 0.41. It assesses government transparency, accountability mechanisms and public participation in policy deliberations.
Bangladesh ranked 107th in order and security, scoring 0.63. The factor measures how effectively a society protects individuals and property.
Despite the annual improvement, Bangladesh's overall rule of law score declined by 0.8% between 2021 and 2026, falling from 0.40 to around 0.39, according to the WJP's country profile.
Six of the index's eight factors deteriorated over the five-year period. Civil justice recorded the sharpest decline at 4.2%, followed by open government at 2.8%, fundamental rights at 1.5%, regulatory enforcement at 0.9%, criminal justice at 0.7% and absence of corruption at 0.2%.
Constraints on government powers and order and security improved by 2.3% and 0.6%, respectively.
Human rights activist and Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Jyotirmoy Barua attributed the deterioration partly to the worsening law and order situation.
"We had expected that an elected government would be able to turn things around to some extent, as the interim government had failed to maintain or restore control over the law and order situation," he said.
"However, the elected government has been trying to bring the entire situation under control at once, and the pressure associated with this has contributed to instability. Law enforcement is also closely linked to the justice system, and our overall performance in these areas has deteriorated," he added.
Nepal remained South Asia's top performer, ranking 71st globally with a score of 0.52, followed by Sri Lanka at 74th and India at 88th. Bangladesh ranked ahead of only Pakistan (131st) and Afghanistan (142nd) in the region.
Denmark topped the 2026 index, followed by Norway, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg. Venezuela ranked last, preceded by Afghanistan, Haiti, Cambodia and Nicaragua.
The index drew on data from more than 215,000 households and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts across 143 countries and jurisdictions. The data were collected between February and August 2026.
The WJP highlighted the links between the rule of law and economic prosperity. Countries with GDP per capita above the global average of $14,406 scored at least 0.68 on the index, while those with inflation below the global median of 3.23% scored at least 0.60. The findings indicate an association between the rule of law, price stability and economic performance.

item.title: UPDF opens fire on tourists, law enforcement personnel in Rangamati's Sajek: ISPR
item.description:
Armed members of the United People's Democratic Front (UPDF) opened fire on tourists and law enforcement in the Gangaram Bazaar area of Sajek, Rangamati district, according to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

The ISPR stated in a press release that the UPDF forcibly used local residents as human shields to block roads.

As a result of the blockage on the Sajek-Baghaihat road, about three thousand tourists visiting Sajek were stranded.

The ISPR press release mentioned that while ensuring the safe passage of tourists, the blockaders created obstacles. In this situation, the Bangladesh Army and police jointly took necessary security measures to ensure the tourists' safe transport to Khagrachari.

While removing the stranded tourists, around 10 AM on Thursday, the blockaders erected barriers in the Gangaram Bazaar area, halting the movement of tourist vehicles. At that time, the army and police patrol team initiated discussions with the blockaders to ensure the safe passage of tourists.

However, during the discussions and around 10: 45 AM, the blockaders, incited by the UPDF, suddenly started throwing stones at law enforcement and targeting tourists, as noted in the statement. To bring the situation under control, the law enforcement used baton charges to disperse the blockaders and resumed the movement of tourist vehicles.

According to the ISPR statement, at approximately 11 AM, it was initially learned that armed UPDF members fired about 30-40 rounds at law enforcement and tourists. During this time, the army patrol team, in self-defense and to ensure the safety of tourists, returned fire, causing the armed individuals to flee the scene. Subsequently, with coordinated efforts by the Bangladesh Army and police, the trapped tourists were evacuated safely, and no casualties were reported.

Preliminary information suggests that the blockade and violence instigated by the UPDF were premeditated. The allegations that locals were coerced into participating in the blockade and being used as human shields are extremely concerning, as mentioned in the statement. It was stated that, due to ongoing security operations in various parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, a faction of UPDF's armed members has taken position in the tourist area.

The statement noted that such violent activities disrupt peace, stability, and public safety in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, and adversely affect the tourism industry and the livelihoods of local people. Especially alarming are incidents endangering the safety of innocent tourists and forcibly involving the general public in the blockade program.

The Bangladesh Army continues its efforts in coordination with the civil administration and other law enforcement agencies to maintain peace, harmony, and stability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and to ensure the safety of the lives and property of local residents and tourists. ISPR informed that the Bangladesh Army will continue its efforts to maintain the peaceful environment of the hill region in the future.

Notably, yesterday, Wednesday, the Sajek Jan Adhikar Raksha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association announced a blockade for the third time on the Sajek tourism road. According to a statement from the organisations, the blockade would continue indefinitely starting today. Therefore, tourists were requested to leave Sajek by yesterday, Wedenday.

Following the blockade call by these regional organisations, the district administration announced the closure of Sajek for safety reasons.

In a public notice last evening, Rangamati Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi stated that the Sajek Valley tourist center in Baghaichhari Upazila would remain temporarily closed until further notice.

item.title: Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
item.description:
FIJI-UN-COP31-CLIMATE-ENVIRONMENT

Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an "extremely high risk" of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned Thursday.

In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet's coral reef systems as "critically endangered" -- its highest risk category.

Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world's oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

"The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

"Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events," said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.

For their assessment, researchers used the "middle-of-the-road" scenario from the UN's panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

The world is on track for 2.6C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned Wednesday.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said in a statement.

Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.

The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63 percent of coral reef ecosystems.

Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.

Critically endangered coral

The IUCN's analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

The world's largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered -- Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.

A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals -- which build its living foundation -- largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.

The report was released during the UN's COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world "are not yet lost".

If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24 percent of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96 percent, the IUCN said.

"It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming," said IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar.

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them."

A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at "elevated relative risk of extinction", with climate change the main driver of this decline.

item.title: PHP security flaw triggers global cyber alert, millions of websites at risk
item.description:
Bangladesh e-Government Computer Incident Response Team (BGd e-GOV CIRT) has issued a high-severity alert over two critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites and web applications.
The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed “PHP2Shell”, could allow hackers to remotely run malicious code on vulnerable servers without a username or password, potentially giving them control of affected systems.
The flaws, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, carry a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score of 9.2 out of 10, placing them in the critical severity category.
According to the alert, the vulnerabilities stem from PHP’s memory management. Attackers could exploit situations involving memory exhaustion or data persisting from previous requests after memory is freed by sending specially crafted HTTP requests to gain control of a server.
Users of PHP-FPM and Apache’s mod_php are particularly at risk. Other potentially affected systems include PHP-CGI, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Docker containers and shared hosting environments. Government portals, banks, e-commerce platforms and websites built on WordPress and Laravel could also be vulnerable.
A successful attack could result in full server compromise, data and file theft, exposure of database passwords and API keys, and website outages, the alert warned.
BGD e-GOV CIRT has urged administrators to update PHP immediately to the secure versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. It also advised them to ensure that the server’s underlying PHP runtime is updated, not just the application framework.
For administrators unable to install the patches immediately, the agency recommended temporarily placing servers behind a VPN, restricting access through IP-based allowlists and increasing log monitoring.
However, BGD e-GOV CIRT stressed that updating PHP is the only permanent solution.
